DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure Proposal (Harbourside Hotel)

**What the paper proposes.** From 1 June, raise the Friday and Saturday Best Available Rate (BAR) from £145 to £165, and require a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday. The case rests on three things:
- a June 2025 rate rise that was followed by higher occupancy;
- strong value-for-money scores;
- rates £20–£35 below competitors.

It projects at least £204,000 a year.

There is a real case for a rise here:
- **Competitors:** their rates of £165–£180 put £165 at the bottom of the range.
- **Demand:** the hotel sold out on 31 Saturdays.
- **Occupancy:** the 2025 average of 79% is calculated correctly.
- **Monitoring:** the plan is reasonable, and compares against the same weeks in 2025.

But the price-sensitivity evidence is confounded by season, the revenue figure uses the wrong room count, and the two-night minimum conflicts with the hotel's biggest source of Saturday business. The £204,000 is not a floor.

## 1. The "price test" coincided with peak season

The rate went up in the last week of June. Occupancy rose from 81% in June to 89% in July. But section 2 itself explains why July is strong: **the harbour festival and the school summer holidays.**

July is always one of the hotel's best months, so the rise tells us nothing about price sensitivity. June was also a dip from May's 85%, which makes the jump look bigger.

**A proper test** would compare July–December 2025 with the same months of 2024, since the rate was £135 before the rise and £145 after. If occupancy held up year on year, that is real evidence.

The value-for-money score of 8.4 doesn't settle it either. It was measured at £145, and it comes from guests who chose to stay. A higher rate may lower it.

## 2. The revenue figure uses the wrong room count and overstates who pays BAR

**Room count.** Section 2 says the hotel has **112 rooms**. Section 5 calculates on **124**.
- 124 × 104 nights × 79% × £20 = £203,757, the paper's figure.
- 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 = **£184,038**.

**Not every weekend room-night pays BAR.** The calculation applies £20 to every occupied weekend room. But many weekend rooms are sold at other rates:
- **Weddings:** about 38% of Saturday bookings are wedding blocks, usually at group rates.
- **Other rates:** some rooms are booked at contracted corporate rates or as packages.
- **OTA bookings:** commission takes a share of every BAR sale through online travel agencies.

**VAT.** If the rates include VAT, as UK rates normally do, £20 on the rate is about £16.67 to the hotel.

**Illustrative effect.** If about 30% of weekend room-nights are not at BAR, and VAT is netted off: 112 rooms × 104 × 79% × 70% × £16.67 ≈ **£107,000**. The real share of non-BAR rooms is in your booking data, so use that.

## 3. The two-night minimum conflicts with weddings

Section 4 notes that wedding guests make up about 38% of Saturday bookings, and that they **arrive on Saturday and leave on Sunday**. A two-night minimum applies directly to them:
- **Future wedding blocks** not yet contracted would face the minimum. The couple, and Quayside Hall, may steer guests to competitors.
- **On sell-out Saturdays,** guests wanting one night may book elsewhere rather than add a Friday or Sunday. That leaves rooms empty or lower-yielding, the opposite of the intended effect.

So the minimum is not guaranteed to add revenue. It could reduce Saturday revenue. That undermines the cover note's "floor" claim, which rests on putting no value on the extra nights the minimum is assumed to create.

**Options:**
- Exempt wedding and group blocks.
- Apply the minimum only on dates forecast to sell out.
- Trial it for a few months first.

## 4. Consider pricing by season

The rise is applied to all 104 weekend nights. Occupancy ranges from 62% in January to 93% in August. A £20 rise on sell-out summer weekends is low risk; in January and February it is riskier. A seasonal or demand-based increase would capture most of the gain with less downside.

## 5. What the rise can absorb

Revenue at the new rate stays level as long as occupancy doesn't fall below about 79% × 145/165 ≈ **69%**, nearly 10 points down. That is a real cushion, and the paper could make that case. The five-point monitoring trigger sits inside it, which is sensible.

But the trigger is on room revenue only. It doesn't count lost spending in the bar and restaurant, or lost wedding referrals.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Existing bookings.** Bookings for June onwards already made at £145 will reduce first-year revenue.
- **Monitoring by month** detects problems a month late. Weekly pick-up, which the paper also mentions, is the better early warning.

## How the cover note differs from the document

| Cover note | The document |
|---|---|
| The June rise "tested" price sensitivity | Confounded with the festival and summer holidays |
| £204,000 is a floor | Uses 124 rooms, not 112; assumes everyone pays BAR |
| The minimum stay only adds revenue | It conflicts with wedding guests, 38% of Saturdays |
| Group commitments are protected | Only blocks already contracted |

## What to fix before approval

1. Use 112 rooms, apply the rise only to the share paying BAR, and state whether figures include VAT.
2. Replace the June-to-July comparison with a year-on-year one.
3. Exempt wedding and group blocks from the minimum stay, or trial it on sell-out dates only.
4. Consider seasonal pricing rather than a flat £20.
5. Present the recommendation as an estimate with a range, not "at least £204,000."

The rate increase is probably justified. The hotel is priced below its competitors and sells out many Saturdays. But the realistic gain is likely nearer £100,000–£180,000 than "at least £204,000," and the two-night minimum needs redesigning around the wedding business.
